vsm1.3:51.1: 9. Books means responsibility for the scriptures.
vsm1.3:51.2: That is an impediment only for one who is constantly busy with recitations, etc., but not for others.
vsm1.3:51.4: The Elder Revata, it seems, the Majjhima reciter, went to the Elder Revata, the dweller in Malaya (the Hill Country),
vsm1.3:51.5: and asked him for a meditation subject.
vsm1.3:51.6: The elder asked him, “How are you in the scriptures, friend?”—”I am studying the Majjhima Nikāya, venerable sir.”
vsm1.3:51.7: —”The Majjhima is a hard responsibility, friend.
vsm1.3:51.8: When a man is still learning the First Fifty by heart, he is faced with the Middle Fifty;
vsm1.3:51.9: and when he is still learning that by heart, he is faced with the Last Fifty.
vsm1.3:51.10: How can you take up a meditation subject?”
vsm1.3:51.11: —”Venerable sir, when I have taken a meditation subject from you, I shall not look at the scriptures again.”
vsm1.3:51.13: and doing no recitation for nineteen years,
vsm1.3:51.14: he reached Arahantship in the twentieth year.
vsm1.3:51.15: He told bhikkhus who came for recitation:
vsm1.3:51.16: “I have not looked at the scriptures for twenty years, friends,
vsm1.3:51.17: yet I am familiar with them. You may begin.”
vsm1.3:51.18: And from beginning to end he had no hesitation even over a single syllable.
vsm1.3:52.1: The Elder Mahā-Nāga, too, who lived at Karuliyagiri (Karaliyagiri) put aside the scriptures for eighteen years,
vsm1.3:52.2: and then he recited the Dhātukathā to the bhikkhus.
vsm1.3:52.3: When they checked this with the town-dwelling elders of Anurādhapura, not a single question was found out of its order.
vsm1.3:53.1:
In the Great Monastery too the Elder Tipiṭaka-Cūḷa-Abhaya had the golden drum struck, saying: “I shall expound the three
Piṭakas in the circle of experts in the Five Collections of discourses,” and this was before he had learnt the commentaries.
vsm1.3:53.4: Unless you give only the teaching of our own teachers we shall not let you speak.”
vsm1.3:53.5: Also his preceptor asked him when he went to wait on him, “Did you have the drum beaten, friend?”
vsm1.3:53.8: —”I shall expound the scriptures, venerable sir.”
vsm1.3:53.9: —”Friend Abhaya, how do the teachers explain this passage?”
vsm1.3:53.10: —”They explain it in this way, venerable sir.”
vsm1.3:53.12: Again three times, each time in a different way, he said, “They explain it in this way, venerable sir.”
vsm1.3:53.14: Then he said, “Friend, your first explanation was the way of the teachers.
vsm1.3:53.15:
But it is because you have not actually learnt it from the teachers’ lips that you
are unable to maintain that the teachers say such and such.
vsm1.3:53.16: Go and learn it from our own teachers.”—”Where shall I go, venerable sir?”
vsm1.3:53.17:
—”There is an elder named Mahā Dhammarakkhita living in the Tulādhārapabbata
Monastery in the Rohaṇa country beyond the Mahaveli River.
vsm1.3:53.20: Saying, “Good, venerable sir,” he paid homage to the elder.
vsm1.3:53.21: He went with five hundred bhikkhus to the Elder Mahā-Dhammarakkhita,
vsm1.3:53.22: and when he had paid homage to him, he sat down.
vsm1.3:53.23: The elder asked, “Why have you come?”—”To hear the Dhamma, venerable sir.”
vsm1.3:53.24: —”Friend Abhaya, they ask me about the Dīgha and the Majjhima from time to time,
vsm1.3:53.25: but I have not looked at the others for thirty years.
vsm1.3:53.26: Still you may repeat them in my presence by night,
vsm1.3:53.27: and I shall explain them to you by day.”
vsm1.3:53.28: He said, “Good, venerable sir,” and he acted accordingly.
vsm1.3:54.1: The inhabitants of the village had a large pavilion built at the door of his dwelling, and they came daily to hear the Dhamma.
vsm1.3:54.2: Explaining by day what had been repeated by night, the Elder Dhammarakkhita eventually completed the instruction.
vsm1.3:54.3: Then he sat down on a mat on the ground before the Elder Abhaya and said,
vsm1.3:54.4: “Friend, explain a meditation subject to me.”
vsm1.3:54.5: —”What are you saying, venerable sir, have I not heard it all from you? What can I explain to you that you do not already know?”
vsm1.3:54.6: The senior elder said, “This path is different for one who has actually travelled by.”
vsm1.3:55.1: The Elder Abhaya was then, it seems, a stream-enterer.
vsm1.3:55.2: When the Elder Abhaya had given his teacher a meditation subject, he returned to Anurādhapura.
vsm1.3:55.3: Later, while he was expounding the Dhamma in the Brazen Palace,
vsm1.3:55.4: he heard that the elder had attained Nibbāna.
vsm1.3:55.5: On hearing this, he said, “Bring me my robe, friends.”
vsm1.3:55.6: Then he put on the robe and said,
vsm1.3:55.7: “The Arahant path befits our teacher, friends.
vsm1.3:55.8: Our teacher was a true thoroughbred.
vsm1.3:55.9: He sat down on a mat before his own Dhamma pupil and said,
vsm1.3:55.11: The Arahant path befits our teacher, friends.”
vsm1.3:55.12: For such as these, books are no impediment.
vsm1.3:56.1: 10. Supernormal powers are the supernormal powers of the ordinary man.
vsm1.3:56.2: They are hard to maintain, like a prone infant or like young corn, and the slightest thing breaks them.
vsm1.3:56.3: But they are an impediment for insight, not for concentration, since they are obtainable through concentration.
vsm1.3:56.4: So the supernormal powers are an impediment that should be severed by one who seeks insight;
vsm1.3:56.5: the others are impediments to be severed by one who seeks concentration.
vsm1.3:56.6: This, in the first place, is the detailed explanation of the impediments.
vsm1.3:57.0: Description of the Giver of a Meditation Subject
vsm1.3:57.1: Approach the good friend, the giver of a meditation subject (§28):
vsm1.3:57.2: meditation subjects are of two kinds, that is,
vsm1.3:57.3: generally useful meditation subjects and special meditation subjects.
vsm1.3:57.4:
Herein, loving-kindness towards the Community of Bhikkhus, etc., and also mindfulness of death
are what are called generally useful meditation subjects.
vsm1.3:57.5: Some say perception of foulness, too.
vsm1.3:58.1: When a bhikkhu takes up a meditation subject,
vsm1.3:58.2:
he should first develop loving-kindness towards the Community of Bhikkhus within the boundary,
limiting it at first to “all bhikkhus in this monastery”, in this way:
vsm1.3:58.3: “May they be happy and free from affliction.”
vsm1.3:58.4: Then he should develop it towards all deities within the boundary.
vsm1.3:58.5: Then towards all the principal people in the village that is his alms resort;
vsm1.3:58.6: then to all human beings there and to all living beings dependent on the human beings.
vsm1.3:58.7: With loving-kindness towards the Community of Bhikkhus he produces kindliness in his co-residents;
vsm1.3:58.8: then they are easy for him to live with.
vsm1.3:58.9: With loving-kindness towards the deities within the boundary he is protected by kindly deities with lawful protection.
vsm1.3:58.10: With loving-kindness towards the principal people in the village that is his alms resort
vsm1.3:58.11: his requisites are protected by well-disposed principal people with lawful protection.
vsm1.3:58.12: With loving-kindness to all human beings there he goes about without incurring their dislike since they trust him.
vsm1.3:58.13: With loving-kindness to all living beings he can wander unhindered everywhere.
vsm1.3:58.16: he gives up improper search (see S II 194; M-a I 115),
vsm1.3:58.17: and with a growing sense of urgency he comes to live without attachment.
vsm1.3:58.18: When his mind is familiar with the perception of foulness, then even divine objects do not tempt his mind to greed.
vsm1.3:59.1:
So these are called “generally useful” and they are “called meditation subjects” since they
are needed generally and desirable owing to their great helpfulness
vsm1.3:59.2: and since they are subjects for the meditation work intended.
vsm1.3:60.1:
What is called a “special meditation subject” is that one from among the forty meditation
subjects that is suitable to a man’s own temperament.
vsm1.3:60.2: It is “special” (pārihāriya) because he must carry it (pariharitabbattā) constantly about with him,
vsm1.3:60.3: and because it is the proximate cause for each higher stage of development.
vsm1.3:60.4: So it is the one who gives this twofold meditation subject that is called the giver of a meditation subject.
vsm1.3:61.1: The good friend is one who possesses such special qualities as these:
vsm1.3:61.2:
He is revered and dearly loved,
And one who speaks and suffers speech;
vsm1.3:61.3:
The speech he utters is profound,
He does not urge without a reason (A IV 32) and so on.
vsm1.3:61.4: He is wholly solicitous of welfare and partial to progress.
vsm1.3:62.1:
Because of the words beginning, “Ānanda, it is owing to my being a good friend to them
that living beings subject to birth are freed from birth” (S I 88),
vsm1.3:62.2: it is only the Fully Enlightened One who possesses all the aspects of the good friend.
vsm1.3:62.3: Since that is so, while he is available only a meditation subject taken in the Blessed One’s presence is well taken.
vsm1.3:62.4: But after his final attainment of Nibbāna, it is proper to take it from anyone of the eighty great disciples still living.
vsm1.3:62.5: When they are no more available,
vsm1.3:62.6:
one who wants to take a particular meditation subject should take it from someone with cankers destroyed,
who has, by means of that particular meditation subject, produced the fourfold and fivefold jhāna,
vsm1.3:62.7: and has reached the destruction of cankers by augmenting insight that had that jhāna as its proximate cause.
vsm1.3:63.1: But how then, does someone with cankers destroyed declare himself thus: “I am one whose cankers are destroyed?”
vsm1.3:63.2: Why not? He declares himself when he knows that his instructions will be carried out.
vsm1.3:63.3:
Did not the Elder Assagutta spread out his leather mat in the air and sitting cross-legged on it
explain a meditation subject to a bhikkhu who was starting his meditation subject, because he knew
that that bhikkhu was one who would carry out his instructions for the meditation subject?
vsm1.3:64.1: So if someone with cankers destroyed is available, that is good.
vsm1.3:64.3:
then one should take it from a non-returner, a once-returner, a stream-enterer, an ordinary man who has obtained jhāna,
one who knows three Piṭakas, one who knows two Piṭakas, one who knows one Piṭaka, in descending order according as available.
vsm1.3:64.4: If not even one who knows one Piṭaka is available,
vsm1.3:64.5:
then it should be taken from one who is familiar with one Collection
together with its commentary and one who is himself conscientious.
vsm1.3:64.6: For a teacher such as this, who knows the texts, guards the heritage, and protects the tradition,
vsm1.3:64.7: will follow the teachers’ opinion rather than his own.
vsm1.3:64.8: Hence the Ancient Elders said three times, “One who is conscientious will guard it.”
vsm1.3:65.1: Now, those beginning with one whose cankers are destroyed, mentioned above,
vsm1.3:65.2: will describe only the path they have themselves reached.
vsm1.3:65.4: his instructions and his answers to questions are purified by his having approached such and such teachers,
vsm1.3:65.5:
and so he will explain a meditation subject showing a broad track, like a big elephant going through a stretch of jungle, and he
will select suttas and reasons from here and there, adding explanations of what is suitable and unsuitable.
vsm1.3:65.6: So a meditation subject should be taken by approaching the good friend such as this, the giver of a meditation subject,
vsm1.3:65.7: and by doing all the duties to him.
vsm1.3:66.1: If he is available in the same monastery, it is good. If not, one should go to where he lives.
vsm1.3:66.2: When a bhikkhu goes to him, he should not do so with feet washed and anointed, wearing sandals,
vsm1.3:66.4: surrounded by pupils, and bringing oil tube, honey, molasses, etc.;
vsm1.3:66.5: he should do so fulfilling the duties of a bhikkhu setting out on a journey,
vsm1.3:66.6: carrying his bowl and robes himself,
vsm1.3:66.7: doing all the duties in each monastery on the way,
vsm1.3:66.9: and living in the greatest effacement.
vsm1.3:66.11:
he should do so expecting nothing, and even provided with a tooth-stick that he
has had made allowable on the way according to the rules.
vsm1.3:66.12:
And he should not enter some other room, thinking, “I shall go to the teacher after resting
awhile and after washing and anointing my feet, and so on.”
vsm1.3:67.2: If there are bhikkhus there who are hostile to the teacher,
vsm1.3:67.3: they might ask him the reason for his coming and speak dispraise of the teacher, saying,
vsm1.3:67.4: “You are done for if you go to him”;
vsm1.3:67.5: they might make him regret his coming
vsm1.3:67.7: So he should ask for the teacher’s dwelling and go straight there.
vsm1.3:68.1: If the teacher is junior, he should not consent to the teacher’s receiving his bowl and robe, and so on.
vsm1.3:68.2: If the teacher is senior, then he should go and pay homage to him and remain standing.
vsm1.3:68.3: When told, “Put down the bowl and robe, friend,” he may put them down.
vsm1.3:68.4: When told, “Have some water to drink,” he can drink if he wants to.
vsm1.3:68.5: When told, “You may wash your feet,” he should not do so at once,
vsm1.3:68.6: for if the water has been brought by the teacher himself, it would be improper.
vsm1.3:68.7: But when told “Wash, friend, it was not brought by me, it was brought by others,”
vsm1.3:68.8: then he can wash his feet, sitting in a screened place out of sight of the teacher,
vsm1.3:68.9: or in the open to one side of the dwelling.
vsm1.3:69.1: If the teacher brings an oil tube, he should get up and take it carefully with both hands.
vsm1.3:69.2: If he did not take it, it might make the teacher wonder, “Does this bhikkhu resent sharing so soon?”
vsm1.3:69.3: but having taken it, he should not anoint his feet at once.
vsm1.3:69.4: For if it were oil for anointing the teacher’s limbs, it would not be proper.
vsm1.3:69.5: So he should first anoint his head, then his shoulders, etc.;
vsm1.3:69.6: but when told, “This is meant for all the limbs, friend, anoint your feet,”
vsm1.3:69.7: he should put a little on his head and then anoint his feet.
vsm1.3:69.8: Then he should give it back, saying when the teacher takes it, “May I return this oil tube, venerable sir?”
vsm1.3:70.1: He should not say, “Explain a meditation subject to me, venerable sir” on the very day he arrives.
vsm1.3:70.2: But starting from the next day, he can, if the teacher has a habitual attendant, ask his permission to do the duties.
vsm1.3:70.3: If he does not allow it when asked, they can be done when the opportunity offers.
vsm1.3:70.4: When he does them, three tooth-sticks should be brought, a small, a medium and a big one,
vsm1.3:70.5: and two kinds of mouth-washing water and bathing water, that is, hot and cold, should be set out.
vsm1.3:70.6: Whichever of these the teacher uses for three days should then be brought regularly.
vsm1.3:70.7: If the teacher uses either kind indiscriminately, he can bring whatever is available.
vsm1.3:71.2: All should be done as prescribed by the Blessed One in the Khandhakas as the right duties in the passage beginning:
vsm1.3:71.3: “Bhikkhus, a pupil should perform the duties to the teacher rightly.
vsm1.3:71.4: Herein, this is the right performance of duties.
vsm1.3:71.5: He should rise early; removing his sandals and arranging his robe on one shoulder, he should give the tooth-sticks
vsm1.3:71.7: and he should prepare the seat.
vsm1.3:71.8: If there is rice gruel, he should wash the dish and bring the rice gruel” (Vin I 61).
vsm1.3:72.1: To please the teacher by perfection in the duties
vsm1.3:72.2: he should pay homage in the evening,
vsm1.3:72.3: and he should leave when dismissed with the words, “You may go.”
vsm1.3:72.4: When the teacher asks him, “Why have you come?” he can explain the reason for his coming.
vsm1.3:72.5: If he does not ask but agrees to the duties being done,
vsm1.3:72.6: then after ten days or a fortnight have gone by
vsm1.3:72.7: he should make an opportunity by staying back one day at the time of his dismissal,
vsm1.3:72.8: and announcing the reason for his coming;
vsm1.3:72.9: or he should go at an unaccustomed time, and when asked, “What have you come for?” he can announce it.
vsm1.3:73.1: If the teacher says, “Come in the morning,” he should do so.
vsm1.3:73.2: But if his stomach burns with a bile affliction at that hour,
vsm1.3:73.3: or if his food does not get digested owing to sluggish digestive heat,
vsm1.3:73.4: or if some other ailment afflicts him,
vsm1.3:73.5: he should let it be known,
vsm1.3:73.6: and proposing a time that suits himself,
vsm1.3:73.7: he should come at that time.
vsm1.3:73.8: For if a meditation subject is expounded at an inconvenient time, one cannot give attention.
vsm1.3:73.9: This is the detailed explanation of the words “approach the good friend, the giver of a meditation subject.”
